mainTopic: רב פפא's unresolved questions about the כפל, then רב הונא's oath for a paying שומר and the lost-משכון משנה
overview: Earlier on the דף we learned that a שומר whose deposit was stolen can pay the owner instead of swearing, and the owner then gives him the right to the כפל, the thief's double payment. On this amud רב פפא asks a long list of questions about when that right still passes to him. What if he said 'I will pay' and then 'I will not pay'? What if he died and his sons refused, or his sons paid, or he paid the owner's sons? What about paying only half, or cases with partners, or with a husband and wife? All of these end with תיקו, with no answer. Then רב הונא rules that even a שומר who offers to pay must swear the item is not with him, in case he wants to keep it. The גמרא quotes a משנה about a lost משכון to test this rule. It explains, with שמואל, that the משנה's rule 'the one holding the deposit swears' refers to the case where the borrower admits part of the claim, and חז"ל moved that oath to the lender. The amud ends as the גמרא starts to ask how this משנה fits with רב הונא, and that question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Saying 'I will not pay': backing out or just delaying?
steps.stepSummary: The שומר first said 'I will pay' and then said 'I will not pay.' Is he backing out of paying, or only putting off the payment?
steps.simpleTranslation: (The שומר said 'I will pay') and then said 'I will not pay.' What is the law? Do we say he is backing out of it? Or maybe he still stands by his word and is only pushing off the owner for now?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רב פפא's question about a שומר who promised to pay and then said he won't. Is that a real backing out, or only a delay?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he really backed out, he never paid, so he has no claim to the כפל. If he still stands by his promise and is just stalling, his original commitment holds, and he may still earn the כפל when he does pay. The whole question is how to read his words 'I will not pay.'

keyTerms.meaning: he is backing out of it
he is putting off (delaying), not refusing

steps.confusionAlert: This text picks up in the middle of רב פפא's question. The first half ('He said: I will pay') appears just before it on the דף.

phrases.english: and then said 'I will not pay,' what is the law?
phrases.notes: The start of the question comes just before this on the דף: the שומר first said 'I will pay.'

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן מִהְדָּר קָא הָדַר בֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: Do we say he is backing out of it,
or perhaps he stands by his word
and he is only putting him off?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אָמְרִינַן מִהְדָּר קָא הָדַר בֵּיהּ, אוֹ דִלְמָא בְּמִלְּתֵיהּ קָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב פפא's question that began just before this text.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'I will not pay' after 'I will pay' cancel the commitment, or is it only a delay?

steps.title: The שומר promised and died, and his sons refuse
steps.stepSummary: The שומר said 'I will pay' and died. His sons say 'We are not paying.' Are they backing out of their father's promise, or only delaying?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said 'I will pay' and died, and his sons said 'We are not paying.' What is the law? Do we say they are backing out? Or maybe they stand by their father's word and are only pushing off the owner for now?
steps.whatsHappening: The same question as before, now about heirs. The father promised, and the sons say they won't pay. Is that a real refusal or just a delay?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the promise was made by one person (the father) and the 'no' comes from others (the sons). The question is whether the sons are cancelling their father's commitment, or still carrying it out and just not paying yet.

phrases.english: He said 'I will pay' and died,
and his sons said 'We are not paying,' what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן מִהְדָּר קָא הָדְרִי בְּהוּ,
phrases.english: Do we say they are backing out of it,
or perhaps they stand by their father's word,
and they are only putting him off?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר הֲרֵינִי מְשַׁלֵּם וָמֵת, וְאָמְרוּ בָּנָיו אֵין אָנוּ מְשַׁלְּמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the backing-out-or-delaying question to the שומר's heirs.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do the heirs' words 'we are not paying' cancel their father's commitment, or are they only a delay?

steps.title: The שומר's sons pay the owner
steps.stepSummary: The sons of the שומר paid the owner. Do they get the כפל, or can the owner say he gave that right only to their father, who did him a favor?
steps.simpleTranslation: If the sons paid, what is the law? Can the owner say to them: 'When I gave away the כפל, it was to your father, because he did me a kindness. To you I did not give it.' Or maybe there is no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question: the שומר's sons pay the owner themselves. Does the right to the כפל pass to them?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows why the owner gives up the כפל in the first place. If it is a personal reward for the kindness of paying quickly, it belongs only to the father who did that kindness. If it is simply a result of being paid, it makes no difference who paid.

keyTerms.meaning: I transferred (the right to) the double payment
peace of mind; a kindness to me

steps.whyThisMatters: This step brings out the reason the owner gives up the כפל: is it a personal reward, or an automatic result of being paid?

phrases.english: If the sons paid, what is the law?
phrases.notes: Here the father died before saying 'I will pay,' and his sons paid the owner.

phrases.english: Can he (the owner) say to them:
When I transferred the double payment,
it was to your father, who gave me peace of mind,
phrases.notes: He means the father did him a favor by paying rather than swearing.

phrases.english: to you, not;
or perhaps there is no difference.

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁלְּמוּ בָּנִים, מַאי? מָצֵי אָמַר לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from heirs refusing to pay to heirs actually paying.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the owner's transfer of the כפל go only to the original שומר, or also to his paying heirs?

steps.title: The שומר pays the owner's sons
steps.stepSummary: The owner died, and the שומר paid the owner's sons. Can the sons refuse to give him the כפל, saying he did the favor for their father and not for them?
steps.simpleTranslation: If he paid the sons, what is the law? Can they say to him: 'Our father gave you the כפל because you did him a kindness, but you did no kindness for us.' Or maybe there is no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The mirror image of the last question. Now the owner is the one who died, and the שומר pays the owner's heirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the question was whether the reward reaches the payer's heirs. Now it is whether the owner's heirs have to grant it. If the כפל is a reward for a personal kindness, the sons could say no kindness was done for them.

keyTerms.meaning: he paid the sons (the owner's heirs)

phrases.english: If he paid the sons, what is the law?
phrases.notes: Here it is the owner who died. The שומר pays the owner's sons.

phrases.english: Can they say to him:
When our father transferred the double payment to you,
it was because you gave him peace of mind,
but us, for us you did not;
or perhaps there is no difference.

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁילֵּם לְבָנִים, מַאי? מָצוּ אָמְרִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Flips step 3: now the receiving side, not the paying side, is the heirs.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can the owner's heirs refuse to give the כפל to a שומר who paid them?

steps.title: Sons pay sons
steps.stepSummary: Both the owner and the שומר died, and the שומר's sons paid the owner's sons. What is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: If sons paid sons, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The last of the questions about heirs puts both sides together: heirs of the שומר pay heirs of the owner. More questions follow in steps 6–8.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This combines the doubts of steps 3 and 4. Here neither the one who did the kindness nor the one who received it is still alive. The גמרא lists more questions before closing all of them with תיקו in step 9.
steps.whatToRemember: All of רב פפא's questions turn on one point. Is the owner's gift of the כפל tied to the commitment and personal kindness of the original שומר, or does it simply follow from the owner being paid? Step 9 ends them all with תיקו.

phrases.english: If sons paid sons, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The שומר's sons are paying the owner's sons, after both fathers have died.

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁלְּמוּ בָּנִים לְבָנִים, מַאי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Combines the two previous cases into one.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the שומר's family get the כפל when his heirs pay the owner's heirs?

steps.title: Paying only part of the value
steps.stepSummary: What if the שומר paid only half, or paid for only one of two borrowed cows?
steps.simpleTranslation: If he paid half, what is the law? If he borrowed two cows and paid for one of them, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps asking about the כפל. Now the שומר paid only part of what he owes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, every case had the שומר paying in full. The question is whether paying only part is enough to earn the כפל, either a share of it or the כפל on the one cow he paid for.

phrases.english: He paid half, what is the law?
He borrowed two cows
and paid for one of them, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁילֵּם מֶחֱצָה, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more questions to the list in steps 1-5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does partial payment earn the כפל, fully or in part?

steps.title: Borrowing from partners or by partners
steps.stepSummary: What if he borrowed from partners and paid only one of them, or partners borrowed and only one of them paid?
steps.simpleTranslation: If he borrowed from partners and paid one of them, what is the law? If partners borrowed and one of them paid, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks two more questions, this time when there are partners on one side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case, only one owner got paid. In the second, only one borrower paid. The question is whether the כפל passes over fully, partly, or not at all when not everyone took part in the payment.

phrases.english: He borrowed from partners
and paid one of them, what is the law?
Partners who borrowed
and one of them paid, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל מִן הַשּׁוּתָּפִין וְשִׁילֵּם לְאֶחָד מֵהֶן, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of questions with cases that involve partners.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does payment by or to only one partner move the כפל?

steps.title: A woman and her husband
steps.stepSummary: What if he borrowed from a woman and paid her husband, or a woman borrowed and her husband paid?
steps.simpleTranslation: If he borrowed from a woman and paid her husband, what is the law? If a woman borrowed and her husband paid, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks its last two questions, which involve a married couple.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the person who paid, or the person who was paid, is the spouse and not the one who made the deal. The גמרא wants to know if that payment counts for the כפל.

phrases.english: He borrowed from a woman
and paid her husband, what is the law?
A woman who borrowed
and her husband paid, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל מִן הָאִשָּׁה וְשִׁילֵּם לְבַעְלָהּ, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the list of questions with cases about husband and wife.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does payment by or to a spouse earn the כפל?

steps.title: All the questions stay unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends with תיקו: none of these questions gets an answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the whole list of questions without answering any of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means the question is left open. It is not a ruling either way. All the questions from step 1 through step 8 remain undecided.

keyTerms.meaning: let it stand; the question stays unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: Every question about when a paying שומר gets the כפל, from backing out to partners to spouses, ends in תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand.
phrases.notes: This one word covers all the questions in the list, not just the last one.

steps.triggerLanguage: תֵּיקוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the series of questions.

steps.title: רב הונא: the שומר must swear the item is not with him
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that even a שומר who offers to pay must swear that the item is not in his possession, because we worry he wants to keep it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא says: We make him swear an oath that it is not in his possession. What is the reason? We worry that maybe he set his eyes on it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רב הונא says that a שומר who agrees to pay must still swear that he does not have the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think that offering to pay ends the matter. רב הונא worries the שומר may like the item and want to keep it by paying its value. The oath stops him from secretly holding onto it.

keyTerms.meaning: he set his eyes on it, he wants it

steps.whyThisMatters: Paying does not let a שומר buy an item against the owner's will. The owner has a right to his actual object.

phrases.english: Rav Huna says:
We make him swear an oath
phrases.notes: This is the שומר who said he would pay instead of swearing.

phrases.english: that it is not in his possession.
What is the reason?
We worry that maybe he set his eyes on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: מַשְׁבִּיעִין אוֹתוֹ שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about the שומר who offers to pay.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שומר who offers to pay must swear that the item is not in his possession.

steps.title: Challenge from a lost משכון: first case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה about a lost משכון in which the borrower goes free without any oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: One who lends to his friend on a משכון, and the משכון was lost, and he says: I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth a שקל. The other one says: No, you lent me a סלע on it and it was worth a סלע. He is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a challenge to רב הונא by quoting a משנה. This step only sets up the source. The actual question comes soon.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender lost the משכון. He says it was worth half the loan, so the borrower still owes half. The borrower says it was worth the full loan, so he owes nothing. He is פטור and does not even need an oath. On the next amud the גמרא will use this משנה to test רב הונא: if the lender has to swear that the משכון is not in his possession, how could he ever bring it out afterward?

keyTerms.meaning: collateral, an item held as security for a loan

phrases.english: They challenged:
One who lends to his friend on a משכון,
and the משכון was lost,
and he says to him: I lent you a סלע on it,
it was worth a שקל.
And the other one says: Not so,
rather, you lent me a סלע on it,
it was worth a סלע. He is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: הַמַּלְוֶה אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ עַל הַמַּשְׁכּוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a challenge to רב הונא from a משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's rule that someone who pays for a lost item must swear that it is not with him.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being set up: the משנה does not seem to call for an oath that the lost משכון is not in the lender's possession.

steps.title: The משכון case continues: partial admission
steps.stepSummary: Same claim, but now the borrower admits the משכון was worth only three דינרים, so he must swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth a שקל. The other one says: No, you lent me a סלע on it and it was worth three דינרים. He is obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps quoting the משנה. It is still setting up the challenge, which begins only in step 20 and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender claims 2 דינרים, which is the gap between a סלע and a שקל. The borrower says the משכון was worth 3, so he admits he owes 1. Because he admits to part of the claim, he is חייב to swear.

keyTerms.meaning: admitting to part of a claim, which brings an oath

steps.confusionAlert: Here חייב means obligated to take an oath, not obligated to pay the full claim.

phrases.english: I lent you a סלע on it,
it was worth a שקל,
and the other one says: Not so,
rather, you lent me a סלע on it,
it was worth three דינרים. He is obligated.
phrases.notes: He admits he owes one דינר out of the two claimed, so he must swear about the rest.

steps.triggerLanguage: סֶלַע הִלְוִיתִיךָ עָלָיו, שֶׁקֶל הָיָה שָׁוֶה, וְהַלָּה אוֹמֵר: לֹא כִי, אֶלָּא סֶלַע הִלְוִיתַנִי עָלָיו, שְׁלֹשָׁה דִּינָרִים הָיָה שָׁוֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second case of the same משנה, still part of the setup.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being set up: the oath in this משנה is about how much was admitted. Nothing is said about the lender swearing that the משכון is not with him.

steps.title: The borrower claims money back and the lender denies it all
steps.stepSummary: The quoted משנה continues with a reverse case: the borrower says the משכון was worth two סלעים, so the lender owes him one. The lender says it was worth only one סלע, so he owes nothing. The lender is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: The borrower says: 'You lent me a סלע on it, and it was worth two.' The other one says: 'No, I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth a סלע.' He is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps quoting the same משנה it is using to challenge רב הונא. Now the borrower is the one making a claim against the lender, and the lender denies all of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower lost a משכון worth two סלעים against a one-סלע loan, so he says the lender owes him the extra סלע. The lender denies the whole claim, and someone who denies everything does not have to take a Torah oath. So he is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: Not so, that is not the case

steps.confusionAlert: The two sides have switched. Earlier the lender was the one claiming money. Here the borrower is the one claiming money from the lender.

phrases.english: "You lent me a סלע on it,
it was worth two"
phrases.notes: He means two סלעים, so the lender owes him back the extra one.

phrases.english: and the other says: "Not so,
rather, I lent you a סלע on it,
it was worth a סלע" – he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: סֶלַע הִלְוִיתַנִי עָלָיו, שְׁנַיִם הָיָה שָׁוֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the same משנה with a reverse case, where the borrower is now the one claiming.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's rule that a שומר must swear the item is not in his possession
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being set up: the משנה is still being quoted. The actual challenge to רב הונא begins only with 'ואם' in step 20.

steps.title: The borrower claims money back and the lender admits part of it
steps.stepSummary: Same claim by the borrower, but now the lender says the משכון was worth five דינרים, which admits he owes one דינר. That is admitting part of the claim, so he must swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: The borrower says: 'You lent me a סלע on it, and it was worth two.' The other one says: 'No, I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth five דינרים.' He is obligated to swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the matching case: the lender now admits to part of what the borrower claims. Because of that, he must take an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סלע is four דינרים. The borrower claims four דינרים back, and the lender admits one of them. That makes him a מודה במקצת, who must take a Torah oath.

keyTerms.meaning: One who admits to part of the claim and must swear on the rest

phrases.english: "You lent me a סלע on it,
it was worth two"
and the other says: "Not so,
rather, I lent you a סלע on it,
it was worth five דינרים" – he is obligated.
phrases.notes: A סלע is four דינרים, so five דינרים means he admits owing one דינר back.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲמִשָּׁה דִּינָרִים הָיָה שָׁוֶה – חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same reverse claim as step 13, but now the lender partly admits it, so he must swear.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This completes the set of cases. The oath here comes from partly admitting the claim, not from any worry that the lender is keeping the item.

steps.title: The one holding the deposit is the one who swears
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends by ruling that the person who had the deposit, the lender, takes the oath. Otherwise the borrower might swear and then the lender could bring out the משכון and show the oath was false.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who swears? The one who has the deposit with him. Otherwise this one might swear, and then the other one would bring out the deposit.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה closes with a rule about who takes the oath, and it gives the reason. This rule is what the גמרא will ask about next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even in a case where the borrower would normally be the one to swear, the oath is moved to the lender, who was holding the משכון. If the borrower swore about its value and the lender then produced it, the borrower's oath could turn out false.

keyTerms.meaning: A deposit (here, the משכון the lender held)
And he will bring out (produce) the item

steps.whyThisMatters: This line is the heart of the discussion. The גמרא needs to pin down which case it refers to before it can decide whether the משנה fits רב הונא's rule.

phrases.english: Who swears?
The one who has the deposit with him.
Otherwise this one might swear
phrases.notes: "This one" is the borrower, who does not have the משכון.

phrases.english: and the other one would bring out the deposit.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי נִשְׁבָּע? מִי שֶׁהַפִּקָּדוֹן אֶצְלוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the משנה with a general rule about who takes the oath.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The holder of the deposit swears, so that the other side does not swear and then get proven wrong when the item is produced.

steps.title: Which case does the oath rule refer to?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which case 'the one who holds the deposit swears' is talking about. It cannot be the last case, because there the lender already has to swear for admitting part of the claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: To which case does it refer? If you say the last case, you could get that rule anyway, since the oath is on the lender because he admits part of the claim!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which part of the משנה the oath rule is meant for. It immediately rules out the last case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the last case (step 14), the lender already swears by Torah law because he admitted part of the claim. The משנה would not need a special rule and a special reason to tell us he swears. So the rule must be about some other case.

keyTerms.meaning: On which one? (Which case is this about?)
The last part of a משנה
You could get it anyway from another reason

phrases.english: To which case does it refer?
If you say it refers to the last case,

phrases.aramaic: וְתִיפּוֹק לֵיהּ דִּשְׁבוּעָה גַּבֵּי מַלְוֶה הִיא,
phrases.english: you could get it anyway, since the oath is on the lender,
because he admits part of the claim!
phrases.notes: This is the five-דינרים case from step 14.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַהֵיָיא? אִילֵּימָא אַסֵּיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks which case the משנה's oath rule from step 15 is about.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case in the משנה the rule 'the holder of the deposit swears' refers to.

steps.title: שמואל: the rule refers to the first case
steps.stepSummary: שמואל answers that the oath rule refers to the first case, where the lender claims more and the borrower admits part.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, שמואל said: it refers to the first case.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the question: the rule about who swears belongs to the first case of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case, the borrower admits part of the lender's claim, so by Torah law the borrower should swear. The משנה teaches that the oath is moved to the lender, who held the משכון, so that the borrower does not swear and then get proven wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of a משנה

steps.whatToRemember: The rule 'the holder of the deposit swears' is a special move of the oath. It applies in the first case, where the borrower would normally be the one to swear, and it shifts the oath onto the lender who held the משכון.

phrases.english: Rather, שמואל said:
It refers to the first case.
phrases.notes: The first case is the one where the lender makes the claim (steps 11–12). Which half of it שמואל means is spelled out in step 19.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The oath rule refers to the first case, where the oath is moved from the borrower to the lender who held the משכון.

steps.title: Which part of the first case did שמואל mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what שמואל meant when he said the oath rule refers to the first case.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'to the first case' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for more detail about שמואל's answer. This question sets up the exact answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case in the משנה has two halves. Saying 'the first case' is not precise enough, so the גמרא asks which half of it שמואל meant.

phrases.english: What does 'to the first case' mean?

steps.title: The oath moves from the borrower to the lender
steps.stepSummary: It is the end of the first case: the lender says the משכון was worth a שקל and the borrower says it was worth three דינרים. The borrower should swear, but חז"ל made the lender swear instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: It means the end of the first case. The lender says: 'I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth a שקל.' The borrower says: 'No, you lent me a סלע on it, and it was worth three דינרים.' Here there is an oath. The oath really belongs to the borrower, but חז"ל said the lender should swear. Otherwise the borrower might swear, and then the lender might bring out the משכון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that שמואל meant the end of the first case. In that case חז"ל moved the oath from the borrower over to the lender.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סלע is four דינרים and a שקל is two. The lender claims two דינרים are still owed. The borrower admits one, so he admits part of the claim (מודה במקצת), and by the basic rule he should swear. But the lender holds the משכון and knows its real value. So חז"ל had him swear, so the borrower would not swear falsely and then be proven wrong when the משכון comes out.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of the first case
A coin worth half a סלע, which is two דינרים
Deposit; here, the משכון the lender was holding

steps.whatToRemember: In the case where the borrower admits part of the claim, the oath should be his. חז"ל moved it to the lender, who held the משכון, so no one swears an oath that the משכון could later prove false.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the lender swears because he is the one admitting part of the claim. Here the borrower is the one admitting part. The lender swears only because חז"ל moved the oath to him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that חז"ל can shift an oath to the person who knows the facts best, even when the basic Torah rule puts it on the other side.

phrases.english: To the last part of the first case:
"I lent you a sela on it,
and it was worth a shekel,"
phrases.notes: A שקל is half a סלע, so the lender says two of the four דינרים are still owed.

phrases.english: and the other one says: "Not so,
rather, you lent me a sela on it,
and it was worth three dinars" — there is an obligation to swear.
For the oath really belongs to the borrower,
but the Rabbis said: let the lender swear,
lest this one, the borrower, swear
and then the other one bring out the deposit.
